articles.headlineTranslated: Wife of the Chairman of the PRC called for global efforts to combat tuberculosis.
articles.summary: Peng Liyuan, wife of the PRC President Xi Jinping and World Health Organization Goodwill Ambassador, urged the international community to support and participate in global TB prevention and treatment. In a written appeal ahead of World Tuberculosis Day on March 24, she highlighted WHO’s substantial work in protecting public health and noted a reversal of the recent global uptick in TB cases. She also marked the 15th anniversary of China’s nationwide volunteer campaign to raise TB prevention and control awareness. Since its launch, more than 1 million volunteers have participated, implementing over 80,000 programs.

articles.headlineTranslated: A special communicable disease control campaign will begin from April 1.
articles.summary: April 1 marks the launch of a special communicable disease control campaign in Gyanpur, Uttar Pradesh, led by District Magistrate Shailesh Kumar and Superintendent of Police Abhinav Tyagi, targeting malaria, dengue, chikungunya, diarrhea, and brain fever (encephalitis). Preparations must be completed before the start, with weekly sanitation, sanitization, and fogging drives. Anti-larval spraying will be carried out in ponds, drains, and canals, and waste disposal improved. Surveillance committees will conduct door-to-door surveys; feverish children will receive medicine kits. Nutritional support will be provided to women and undernourished children. Rural areas will prioritize cleaning ponds, streams, and drains; urban bodies must test hand-pump water and clean overhead tanks, aiming to surpass last year’s performance. All activities should be reported via WhatsApp groups. Key officials present included CMO Dr. Santosh Kumar Chak, PD Atdiy Kumar, DIOs Anshuman, BSA Shivam Pandey, and District Malaria Officer RamAasre Pal.

articles.headlineTranslated: Miklós Rusvai Revealed: Could the Next Global Pandemic Come? | Economx
articles.summary: Nipah virus in India triggers quarantine for over 100 people; virologist Miklós Rusvai states global spread is unlikely. The virus is carried by fruit bats endemic to Southeast Asia, transmitted to humans occasionally; human-to-human spread is very limited and requires extremely close contact, unlike coronavirus. Nipah infection presents with fever, respiratory distress and encephalitis, potentially leading to coma; diagnosed cases have roughly a 50% case-fatality rate. Many infections may be asymptomatic. There is no antiviral treatment; recovery spans about two weeks, but survivors may suffer long-term neurological sequelae. Bats can carry other pathogens such as Ebola and rabies; deforestation has increased bat–human contact, particularly in tropical regions. The article emphasizes that, despite severe outbreaks, this is not expected to become a global pandemic.

articles.headline: Diarrhoea outbreak at residential complex in Goa, water contamination suspected
articles.summary: Diarrhoea outbreak in Goa's Dabolim, South Goa district, at the Prabhu Violetta residential complex (nearly 200 flats) with 149 cases reported in a week as of 19 March 2026. Affected include children and elderly; symptoms include vomiting, dehydration and severe abdominal pain, with several hospitalised. A house-to-house survey by Cortalim Primary Health Centre since 14 March identified 149 cases, including three on 17 March. Suspected water contamination; samples collected from multiple points inside the complex — a residential flat, underground sump supplying tap water, a swimming pool, and treated sewage lines used for gardening. Goa State Pollution Control Board carried out independent inspection and sampling. Builder Prabhu Realtors is accused of illegal discharge of untreated sewage within the complex. Medical officer in charge Dr Tejan Lotlikar directed halting borewell water supply to residents until test reports are available; the contamination source remains under investigation.

articles.headline: 20,000 birds to be culled in Alappuzha & Kozhikode amid bird flu outbreak
articles.summary: Highly pathogenic avian influenza (H5N1) detected in birds in Kerala's Alappuzha and Kozhikode districts. In Kozhikode, infections reported in Olavanna, Kakkodi, Panangad, Perumanna panchayats and Nallalam; in Alappuzha, Muhamma panchayat. A culling operation targets over 20,000 birds: 14,228 in Kozhikode and 5,961 in Alappuzha, beginning March 21 within a one-kilometre radius of affected sites, under rapid response teams. National and international avian influenza protocols guide the response; a second phase will include mopping and combing to remove hidden birds. Lab confirmation came from the National Institute of High Security Animal Diseases in Bhopal. So far the outbreak is restricted to birds. Surveillance zones impose bans on sale/transport/use of poultry, eggs, meat until further notice; cooking poultry at 70°C for 3–5 minutes is deemed safe. Public urged to report mass bird deaths; PPE, deep burial, and disinfectants recommended for carcass handling. A Kozhikode control room coordinates cross-department efforts.

articles.headline: Do Nipah vírus à gripe aviária: há uma nova pandemia à vista? | Com a Palavra
articles.headlineTranslated: From Nipah virus to avian flu: is there a new pandemic on the horizon? | Com a Palavra
articles.summary: Nipah virus triggers a 2026 global alert: first identified in Malaysia in 1998, it spilled from fruit bats to pigs and then to humans, with outbreaks especially in India. It now shows potential direct bat-to-human transmission, with mortality reaching 75%, but limited human-to-human spread probably prevents a pandemic. The episode underscores wildlife–human interfaces as a source of dangerous pathogens. Avian influenza A(H5N1) looms as a pandemic threat if the virus gains sustained human transmission, particularly amid perceived gaps after recent declines in U.S. surveillance. Measles resurges as vaccination coverage falls: the United States faces its largest outbreak in decades; Bolivia is a neighboring hotspot, and measles has been the leading cause of death among children in Brazil. A highly globalized world enables rapid cross-border spread; without robust surveillance and vaccination, the next pandemic threat could arrive sooner than expected.

articles.headline: Plan to round up millions of dogs sparks 'global health' warning
articles.summary: Delhi, India faces a controversial plan to confine millions of stray dogs in mega shelters, up to 5,000 per site, after a 2025 Supreme Court order. The move targets a city of more than 33 million residents amid ongoing rabies concerns; India's stray dog population is estimated at 15–60 million nationwide. More than 2,000 experts warn mass detention could trigger zoonotic outbreaks that spread beyond borders, turning shelters into high-risk biohazard zones. Critics say removing vaccinated dogs could reverse a 75% drop in human rabies since 2003 and weaken herd immunity, while dogs currently act as a bio-buffer limiting disease-carrying wildlife such as rats, leptospirosis and plague. Costs could exceed ₹6,000 crore over a decade, potentially diverting funds from sanitation and health programs. Scientists advocate expanding sterilization and vaccination to at least 70% rather than detention.

A Kozhikode control room coordinates public assistance, PPE use, and deep burial/disinfection of carcasses.

articles.headlineTranslated: Khangva disease wreaks havoc, three cattle die.
articles.summary: Three cattle have died and about a dozen are affected by Khangva disease in GobariDih village, Bengabad, with scattered cases in other villages of the block over the past two weeks. Symptoms begin as leg infections that progress to large wounds; poor cleaning allows maggots to proliferate, and their activity leads to mouth lesions as cattle lick the wounds. Affected animals stop eating, saliva drips, and water intake falls, culminating in death for some. The outbreak is escalating as the veterinary department in Bengabad has taken no concrete containment steps; farmers lack access to government veterinary facilities and resort to private practitioners. Attempts to contact the block veterinary officer, Dr. Jyoti Kujur, via mobile on Thursday at 2:56 PM were unsuccessful. The crisis is causing substantial livestock losses and threatening livelihoods in Bengabad and neighboring villages.

articles.headline: Why the Bay Area has been a tuberculosis hotspot for more than a century
articles.summary: TB remains a Bay Area hotspot, with Alameda, Santa Clara, San Francisco, and San Mateo counties among California’s top 10 for cases, with rates up to three times the national average. San Francisco recently faced an outbreak affecting more than 200 high school students. Over 90% of active Bay Area cases occur among immigrants from countries with limited vaccine access, highest among those born in the Philippines and Vietnam, followed by India, China, and Mexico. Alameda County outbreaks center in Oakland’s Chinatown; Daly City accounts for about 45% of San Mateo’s cases, and San Jose had the second-highest city-rate in the U.S. metro area in 2021. Nearly two-thirds of active cases involve people who have lived in the U.S. for more than 10 years. articles.headlineTranslated: Natural supplement urgently recalled after contamination with a deadly bacterium. Dozens of people have been hospitalized.
articles.summary: Salmonella contamination linked to moringa-based dietary supplements has sickened about 100 people and led to more than 20 hospitalizations across 32 U.S. states, tied to Live it Up Super Greens and Why Not Natural sold online from 2024 through early 2026. CDC and FDA confirm Salmonella Typhimurium and Salmonella Newport in ingredients and finished products; one outbreak strain was found in moringa leaf powder and in an opened Why Not Natural bottle, with additional detections in Live it Up products, indicating contamination in the production chain. Investigations point to a common producer and shared moringa sources from India. Recalls target Live it Up lot codes starting with 'A' and the cited Why Not Natural lot; products distributed online via Amazon, with UK distribution noted and possible unauthorized cross-border sales (eBay, Walmart). Symptoms appear 12-72 hours after consumption; severe cases may require hospitalization. Seek medical care if symptomatic; online orders could reach Romania despite no official market listing.

articles.headline: Recent Legionnaire's Disease Outbreaks In London, New York Raise Alarm: Is India At Risk?
articles.summary: Legionnaires’ disease outbreaks have surged in London and New York City. In NYC, dozens of infections and multiple deaths have been reported, linked to contaminated cooling towers atop buildings including hospitals and construction sites; several cooling towers tested positive, highlighting inspection and disinfection lapses. London investigations point to large interconnected urban water systems as the likely source. Legionnaires’ disease, caused by Legionella pneumophila, spreads via inhalation of contaminated water droplets, not person-to-person; incubation 2–14 days; symptoms include high fever, cough, shortness of breath, muscle aches, headaches, with nausea or confusion in severe cases. Mortality around 5–10%, higher for older adults, smokers, and immunocompromised. Prevention centers on managing water systems: regular cooling tower cleaning, keeping hot water above 60°C and cold water below 20°C, preventing stagnation, disinfecting large plumbing, and risk assessments. India has sporadic cases; underdiagnosis is suspected; past Indore incidents illustrate vulnerability; preventive measures urged.

articles.headline: NIH Advances Nipah Vaccine for 2029 Clinical Trials
articles.summary: NIH advances Nipah vaccine and treatment, with vaccine trials targeted for 2029 and therapeutic trials for 2032, as Nipah’s fatality can reach 75%. KDCA designated Nipah infection as a Category 1 notifiable disease in Sept 2025, the first new designation since COVID-19 in Jan 2020. Nipah is a priority pathogen under NIH’s 2023 preparedness plan. Vaccine platforms include recombinant proteins and mRNA; in-house animal studies show cellular immune responses, and IVI confirms immunogenicity with a Nipah pseudovirus. Timeline: 2026–2028 animal-model efficacy and safety evaluations; Phase 1 trials 2029–2030; first domestically developed Nipah vaccine expected. Therapeutic candidates identified by 2026, with non-clinical work through 2029 and IND for Phase 1 in 2032. Nipah is a zoonotic virus with fruit bats as natural hosts; early symptoms include fever, headache, vomiting, dizziness, progressing to acute encephalitis and possible coma or death within 24–48 hours. Malaysia 1998 outbreak: 265 infected, 105 deaths (39.6%); early 2026 cases in West Bengal, India; KDCA measures include reporting and isolation; WHO/CEPI designate Nipah as a priority pathogen with pandemic potential.

articles.headline: Temporal dynamics of malaria in Mizoram: a district wise analysis - Journal of Parasitic Diseases
articles.summary: Mizoram, a northeastern Indian state, bears a high malaria burden, with persistent Pf prevalence and high API. Analyzing district-level data from 2011–2020, the study tracks Total Malaria Cases (TMC), % Plasmodium falciparum, API, Total positivity Rate (TPR), ABER, and malaria deaths. Lawngtlai, Lunglei, and Mamit are the top three districts by average malaria cases; Champhai records the lowest. Mamit reports the highest malaria deaths. Age analysis shows malaria prevalence peaks at 15 years and older, lowest in 0–4 years. The incidence peak occurred in 2015 across age groups and sexes. In Lawngtlai, TMC significantly correlates with API and TPR. District-wise, Lawngtlai differs from Mamit, Saiha, and Serchhip (p<0.01). The findings support intensified surveillance, targeted vector control, improved diagnosis/treatment access, and community education to guide policy under Mizoram’s State Vector Borne Diseases Control Programme.

articles.headlineTranslated: Mpox evolves: new strain concerns health authorities.
articles.summary: As of March 18, 2026, the World Health Organization warns of a putative new mpox variant arising from recombination between clades Ib and IIb, with the possibility of silent circulation. Two cases have been identified: the first in India with symptom onset in September 2025, and a second in the United Kingdom, with no evidence of transmission among close contacts. Initial analyses indicate preserved replication capacity, but it remains unclear whether the variant is more transmissible or more severe, and recombination may complicate detection by standard tests. Separately, a study in The New England Journal of Medicine questions tecovirimat's efficacy against mpox, reporting no significant reduction in recovery time in immunocompetent patients. The WHO urges heightened surveillance, genomic sequencing, contact tracing, and vaccination of vulnerable groups, noting that ongoing evolution requires close monitoring despite no clear increase in disease severity yet.

articles.summary: 149 suspected diarrhoea cases were reported from the Prabhu Violetta building in Dabolim, Vasco, Goa, with water contamination suspected from bore wells within the complex. Portable water supplied by the PWD is for kitchen use only; bore water is used for other purposes. The Goa State Pollution Control Board and the FDA are involved in the investigation.

articles.summary: March 18, 2026: Kangra district in Himachal Pradesh aims to achieve tuberculosis (TB)-free status through coordinated action and participation. Additional Deputy Commissioner Vinay Kumar chaired the Multi-Sectoral TB-Free India Campaign and the District TB Eradication Committee at Zonal Hospital, Dharamshala. AI-based assessment identified 969 high-risk villages and wards, with focused screening underway; about 1.56 lakh vulnerable individuals have been screened, while remaining population testing continues. 287 panchayats have been declared TB-free. More than 400 TB champions are spreading awareness. The strategy prioritizes upfront NAAT testing based on key symptoms and X-ray screening for vulnerable groups, alongside 100% case notification, contact tracing, and TB preventive treatment. Modern tools, including portable X-ray and NAAT machines, enhance rapid diagnosis; proper nutrition remains vital. NITI Aayog lauded Kangra’s public participation model under TB-Free India Campaign 2.0. Campaigns target slums, construction sites, transport hubs, and migrant populations; nutrition kits distributed under the Nikshay Mitra Scheme.

Eradication would protect dairy supply chains and export potential.

articles.summary: Eight-year-old boy from Kotilingala village, Velgatoor mandal, Jagtial district, died after about 15 months of rabies following a stray dog bite in December 2024. Vaccinated in Hyderabad, infection progressed to spinal cord and brain, with respiratory distress after Sankranti holidays; he died despite prolonged ventilator-supported treatment at corporate hospitals. Family spent Rs 60–70 lakh. In a separate case, a two-year-old girl in the 29th division of Ramannapet, Warangal, was injured by a stray dog and is receiving treatment for arm injuries. Residents demand stricter stray dog population control amid rising safety concerns in the region.

articles.headline: National Workshop Charts Roadmap for Pandemic Preparedness and Zoonotic Surveillance | Law-Order
articles.summary: Two-day national workshop in Nagpur, organized by NIOH (DHR, MoHFW) with ICMR-RMRC Bhubaneswar, advanced Operational Frameworks for One Health: National Vision and State Action to translate the National One Health Mission (NOHM) into state- and district-level actions. Prof. Ajay Sood framed One Health as the foundation of India’s health security and future pandemic preparedness, noting ecological diversity and the human–animal interface and urging interoperable surveillance with seamless data flow; Maharashtra was cited as a potential model for structured implementation. Dr. Rajiv Bahl described NOHM as a whole-of-government framework to manage zoonotic risks and called for state- and district-level outbreak response teams for faster detection and containment. India faces a rising burden of zoonoses (60–70% of emerging infectious diseases globally); climate change, urbanization, and increased human–wildlife interaction amplify risks. NOHM aligns with WHO/FAO/UNEP, emphasizing multi-sectoral collaboration across health, agriculture, environment, and governance.

articles.summary: Dengue and malaria cases are rising rapidly in Jaunpur, India, as heat and humidity boost mosquito breeding. Dirty water, open drains, and poor sanitation create ideal breeding sites for mosquitoes, elevating risk of dengue, malaria, and chikungunya. Common symptoms include high fever, headache, body pains, vomiting, weakness, and reduced platelets; dengue can be severe without timely treatment. Preventive measures include eliminating standing water from coolers, flower pots, tires, and roof vessels; weekly water cleaning; using bed nets at night; wearing full-coverage clothing; employing mosquito-repellent creams or devices. If fever, body pain, or weakness persists, seek immediate medical care; avoid self-medication. Health department campaigns are underway, but public vigilance is essential to curb mosquito-borne diseases during this season.

articles.headline: When Hospitals Make Patients Sicker: The Hidden Risk Of Hospital-Acquired Infections
articles.summary: Hospital-Acquired Infections (HAIs) are rising globally, affecting up to 15% of patients in low- and middle-income countries who acquire infections during hospitalization, typically 48 hours after admission. Infections include bloodstream infections, pneumonia, surgical-site infections, and urinary tract infections, increasingly driven by antibiotic-resistant organisms such as MRSA. The issue extends beyond clinical protocols to the hospital environment: hygiene lapses, surface and air quality, equipment handling, and especially textile management, with bedsheets and gowns acting as silent carriers without proper segregation, thermal disinfection, and processing. A single HAI can extend a hospital stay by up to 20 days, increase antibiotic use, and fuel antimicrobial resistance. Solutions require measurable hygiene with continuous monitoring of wash temperatures, chemical dosing, and sterilisation cycles, and accountability among doctors, nurses, staff, and visitors. Examples cited include India’s AIMS Hospital, Dombivli, and insights from Anshul Gupta (Quick Clean).

articles.headline: The Hindu's editorial in Hindi | ​Prison outbreak: On the health crisis in India's prisons
articles.headlineTranslated: Prison outbreak: On the health crisis in India's prisons.
articles.summary: HSV outbreak at Jalpaiguri Central Correctional Home, West Bengal, infected 92 inmates and caused 7 deaths between Aug 20, 2025 and Mar 9, 2026; crowded, poorly sanitized conditions hinder isolation and raise encephalitis risk in immunocompromised inmates. Indian prisons operate well above capacity: West Bengal district jails >160% full; Kandi Sub-Jail historically >400%. Kerala (2023) saw 30% of inmates with skin diseases. Lancet Public Health 2023 found prisoners have fivefold TB risk vs general population; 2025 MoHA ordered TB screening camps due to rapid spread in non-ventilated environments. Nagpur and Indore central jails previously experienced major COVID-19 outbreaks. HIV prevalence among inmates is higher than the national average, linked to intake screening gaps; 43% health posts vacant; doctor-to-prisoner ratio 2.6x the ideal; 25 psychologists for 570,000 inmates. Recommendations: link prisons to the National Health Mission, hire trained staff, standardize health protocols, expedite judicial processes, and accelerate deportation of foreign nationals where appropriate.

articles.summary: Gandhi Medical College, Bhopal, is developing a sentinel surveillance site to monitor zoonotic diseases, including rabies, scrub typhus, brucellosis, and leptospirosis. Scrub typhus is a deadly fever spread by mites; rabies is a fatal virus transmitted through the saliva of dogs and wild animals; brucellosis spreads via direct animal contact or contaminated dairy products; leptospirosis transmits through rats and contaminated water. The center will function as a sentinel, issuing early warnings when one or two suspected cases are detected in the region, enabling health authorities to deploy vector control, vaccination, or other containment measures promptly. It will also provide free access to expensive private-lab tests for the public. Dr. Kavita N. Singh, Dean, Gandhi Medical College, notes the data will help build solid strategies to prevent animal-to-human infections at an early stage.

On March 18, health officials collected four more samples; two could not provide due to being outside the city. The department will send the specimens to KGMU and test the infected individuals’ family members, with results expected in 2–3 days to clarify the situation.

articles.headlineTranslated: Nipah virus vaccines and therapeutics development pushed forward... phased clinical trials to begin three years from now
articles.summary: Nipah virus vaccines and therapeutics development is advancing at Korea’s National Institute of Health (NIH). Nipah is a zoonotic infection transmitted from fruit bats with human-to-human potential; case fatality ranges from 40% to 75%. Historical outbreaks include Malaysia (1998): 265 infections, 105 deaths (39.6% CFR); India (2007): 5 infections, all fatal. In 2026, West Bengal, India reported Nipah cases, rekindling global attention; WHO and CEPI classify Nipah as a priority pathogen with pandemic potential. No licensed vaccines or treatments exist. NIH aims to have a domestic Nipah vaccine enter clinical trials by 2029 and a therapeutic by 2032, using recombinant protein and mRNA platforms. Preclinical animal studies show basic efficacy; IVI pseudovirus testing confirms immunogenicity. Timeline: animal efficacy this year; safety assessments 2027–2028; Phase 1 trials 2029–2030; therapeutics discovery through 2029 with nonclinical work to 2029 and IND submission by 2032. NIH Director Nam Jae-hwan calls for expanded domestic and international collaboration.

articles.summary: Cholera outbreak in Jabalpur during the 1920s led British authorities to lease tracts in Napier Town, Right Town, and Gol Market. While cholera subsided, the colonial-era lease system persists, forcing residents to navigate a registry process tied to municipal lease taxes. Napier Town is now Dayanand Saraswati Ward, Right Town Subhadra Kumari Chauhan Ward, Gol Market Bhawani Prasad Tiwari Ward, but lease terms remain unchanged. For residential plots, 4% lease tax; for commercial land up to 8%; plus standard registry fees, a large portion of sale proceeds goes to the municipality. Opposition leader Amrish Mishra notes the 90-year lease has ended and been reduced to 30 years by the city corporation. As of March 2026, many residents demand freehold and the removal of the lease regime, arguing bureaucratic hurdles persist despite name changes.

articles.summary: TB is rising in Malaysia, with Dr. Syed Anwar warning that tuberculosis can cause permanent lung damage and may spread to the brain or spinal cord, potentially fatal. In two weeks, Malaysia reported about 600 new TB cases; by February 21, more than 3,000 confirmed positives identified. articles.headline: Biosecurity to be tightened after bird flu outbreak kills 8,500 poultry birds at Bihar govt farms
articles.summary: An H5N1 avian influenza outbreak in Bihar has killed about 8,500 poultry birds on government farms as of 17 March 2026, with 6,000 deaths at BASU’s Poultry Research Training Centre in Kaushal Nagar, Chitkohra, and 2,500 at the Livestock Farm Complex near Patna airport. Bird flu was confirmed on 12 March, prompting a 1-km culling radius and the culling of about 210 birds at the ICAR campus on 14 March; a February 25 cull of roughly 5,000 birds at BASU preceded this. Eight districts—Patna, Bhojpur, Saran, Bhagalpur, Darbhanga, Katihar, West Champaran, and Banmankhi (Purnia)—have reported infections; Patna has infections in both poultry and crows, others mainly in crows with 400+ deaths. Migratory birds are suspected carriers. BASU will tighten biosecurity (pruning trees, dedicated labor, changing clothes, uniform age groups), install ultrasonic deterrents, segregate stock, and shift birds to Jamui and Kishanganj; private partnerships may house up to 2,000 birds to sustain research.

articles.summary: Ernakulam district in Kerala records the state's highest hepatitis A burden, with more than 150 cases per month and over 80 cases reported in 16 days of March 2026. Kalamassery, with a history of outbreaks and a floating population, has conducted mass chlorination and health education to mitigate spread. Officials urge alertness during summer and monsoon and emphasize water treatment.

articles.headline: ​Prison outbreak: on the health crisis in India's prisons
articles.summary: HSV outbreak at Jalpaiguri Central Correctional Home (West Bengal) infected 92 inmates from Aug 20, 2025 to Mar 9, 2026, with seven deaths; overcrowding (171% occupancy) hindered hygiene and isolation. West Bengal prisons routinely exceed 160% occupancy; Kandi Sub-Jail has exceeded 400%. Across India, 2023 Kerala prisons reported 30% inmates with skin diseases linked to humidity and crowding. A 2023 Lancet Public Health study found Indian prisoners five times more likely to develop tuberculosis than the general population; 2025 Home Ministry ordered prison TB screening camps. Nagpur and Indore central jails experienced major COVID-19 outbreaks. HIV prevalence among inmates is higher than the national average due to shared equipment and inadequate entry screening; 43% vacancy rate for medical officers yields 2.6 inmates per doctor. Only 25 psychologists for 570k inmates. Recommendations: integrate prisons into National Health Mission; hire more health workers; fast-track undertrial cases; expand bail/non-custodial options; repatriate foreign nationals.

articles.headline: Rising rabies cases in Karwar trigger vigil along border | Goa News - The Times of India
articles.summary: Rabies surveillance along South Goa’s border has intensified after a rise in canine rabies cases in Karnataka’s Karwar. Mission Rabies data show Karwar reported 45 rabies-positive dogs in 2025; 2026 so far records 15 cases, raising spillover concerns into Canacona. Officials warn that ongoing canine rabies near the interstate boundary poses a risk if not contained through timely vaccination, surveillance, and reporting. Authorities are expanding border monitoring, deploying field teams, and coordinating with Karwar district officials for a joint response. The strategy prioritizes expanding stray-dog vaccination campaigns, increasing surveillance officers in sensitive border zones, and improving early detection and reporting mechanisms, according to Murugan Appupillai, director of education, Mission Rabies Goa. Sawantwadi reportedly sees relatively stable numbers; underreporting is suspected. No human infections have been reported; current focus remains canine, with additional personnel and community engagement planned.

articles.summary: Kyasanur Forest Disease (KFD) in Shivamogga, Karnataka, is being tackled with enhanced control measures as ticks remain active November–May, peaking January–March. Deputy Commissioner Prabhulinga Kavalikatti directs awareness campaigns, fever surveys, immediate treatment of fever cases, and reserving 10 beds in each taluk hospital for KFD patients. Surveillance in the Malnad region, especially hotspots with monkey deaths, is prioritized; multi-department coordination (Health, Animal Husbandry, Forest, Rural Development, Panchayat Raj) is emphasized. Public guidance includes using tick repellent oil (DEPA). Monkey deaths are an early warning; autopsies confirmed KFD in 31 of 114 observed monkey deaths. Abhishek, K.S. Nataraj.

articles.headline: Measles Data and the Critical Impact of Global Travel on Disease Resurgence, Highlighting the Intersection of Health and Tourism - Travel And Tour World
articles.summary: Measles remains an exceptionally contagious respiratory virus, with airborne persistence up to two hours. Despite US elimination in 2000, sporadic outbreaks and imported cases persist. CDC reports 2024 had 285 confirmed cases; by March 12, 2026, 1,362 cases across 31 jurisdictions, including California, Florida, New York City, and Texas, with about 94% linked to outbreaks. Most infections occur in unvaccinated or vaccination-unknown individuals. Global travel, international airports, cruise ships, and crowded tourist sites drive transmission, with many cases imported by travelers returning from abroad or visitors, including VFR travelers. Globally, outbreaks are noted in Yemen, India, Indonesia, and Pakistan. Measles can cause pneumonia, encephalitis, and permanent hearing loss; mortality is ~1–3 per 1,000 children. Two-dose MMR is ~97% effective; herd immunity of 95% is needed. Vaccination, laboratory support, diagnostics, and travel guidance from the CDC are critical as travel volumes rise and importation risk remains high.

Two-dose MMR lowers exposure risk from about 90% to 3%, thereby reducing SSPE risk.

articles.summary: Rajasthan launches the seventh phase of the Foot-and-Mouth Disease (FMD) control program, aiming to vaccinate over 23.2 million (2.32 crore) dairy animals to safeguard livestock health and the dairy sector. FMD is a highly contagious viral illness affecting cloven-hoofed livestock such as cattle, buffalo, sheep, and goats, causing fever, mouth ulcers, and excessive drooling, with milk production declines. The vaccination drive operates in mission mode, employing ear tagging for individual identification and digital tracking on the INAPH portal to monitor coverage. Veterinary teams are conducting village-to-household vaccination, ensuring stocks and maintaining the cold chain, with awareness camps to reach all eligible animals. articles.headline: Doctors warn of a deadly complication from measles outbreaks
articles.summary: Deepanwita Dasgupta, 8, from Bangalore, began stumbling at age 5; a spinal tap showed measles in her cerebrospinal fluid, leaving her paralyzed and nonverbal. Measles complications affect about 3 in 10 infections, with subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) a rare, fatal brain disorder that typically appears years after infection. Risk is higher if infection occurs before age 5; endemic countries like India see cases routinely. In the United States, falling vaccination rates raise concern for SSPE as outbreaks continue. Since 2025, CDC reports more than 3,500 measles cases, mostly among unvaccinated children; Connecticut diagnosed a 6-year-old with SSPE, and a California child who had measles as an infant died. Two-dose MMR reduces exposure infection risk from ~90% to ~3%, lowering SSPE risk. A 2017 California study found SSPE in about 1 per 1,400 measles cases under 5, and 1 per 600 infected babies. Herd immunity around 95% is urged.

articles.headline: The link between antimicrobial resistance and seasonal change: Prevalence of ARGs, stress resilience, virulence and plasmids in raw milk Escherichia coli of Gujarat, India - AMR Insights
articles.summary: Escherichia coli isolated from raw milk in Gujarat, India shows seasonal variation in antimicrobial resistance (AMR), virulence traits, and genomic profiles. The study combined phenotypic testing with whole-genome sequencing to assess how seasons shape resistance and adaptation. Resistance peaks during summer and monsoon seasons, while key resistance genes blaCTX-M-15 and qnrS1 are detected year-round and often plasmid-borne, indicating a strong potential for horizontal gene transfer. Seasonal differences also appear in stress tolerance and virulence factors, suggesting environmental conditions drive bacterial adaptation in dairy ecosystems. The findings call for season-aware AMR surveillance and One Health strategies linking food production, environmental reservoirs, and human health, particularly regarding plasmid-mediated ESBL and fluoroquinolone resistance in raw-milk–associated E. coli in Gujarat.

articles.headlineTranslated: 24 organizations warn about the "start" of a yellow fever epidemic and call for transparency.
articles.summary: Twenty-four organizations, led by the National Academy of Medicine and the NGO Provea, warn of the start of a yellow fever epidemic in Venezuela and urge immediate government action. They criticize opacity, noting first cases were detected in June 2025 but eight months passed before acknowledgment. In a letter to the Health Ministry and Parliament, experts urge release of the 2024–2026 epidemiological bulletins to restore transparency and evidence-based decisions. Health Minister Nuramy Gutiérrez confirmed deaths from the disease last year, while official tallies show seven confirmed cases in 2026; Isabel Iturria had cited 36 infections since mid-2025. The government declared an epidemiological alert aiming for 95% vaccination coverage, reporting 49,000 recently immunized, adding to about three million vaccinated over the past decade, with donations from India, Russia and Brazil. Despite efforts, the Expanded Immunization Program has not met targets, underscoring the need to strengthen health systems to reach all Venezuelans.
